title: Calf pain in a young woman on the pill
desc: This station involves a focused history and examination of a 26-year-old woman with two days of left calf pain, then interpreting her observations, a compression ultrasound with Doppler and baseline bloods, applying the Wells score, planning anticoagulation and contraception in general practice, and safety-netting.
focus: Unilateral calf pain: VTE risk factor history, Wells score, compression ultrasound and outpatient DVT management
stem: You are a medical student on your general practice rotation. Mary Schulz, a 26-year-old accountant, has come to see her GP about pain in her left calf. Your GP supervisor has asked you to see her first.
tasks: Take a focused history from Mary about her presenting complaint and perform a focused examination, telling the examiner what you are examining and why (10 minutes).
The examiner will give you Mary's observations, her leg ultrasound report and her blood results. Interpret them, then outline your management approach and your safety netting (5 minutes).
patient:
Role: You are Mary Schulz, 26, an accountant. You are a bit anxious and keen to get back to work. The examiner gives examination findings from the Exam findings below when the candidate says what they would examine.

Opening line: "I've had this pain in my left calf for a couple of days and it just isn't going away."

The pain (give only when asked):

  • Site: the back of your left calf only. It does not spread anywhere. The right leg is fine.
  • Character: a deep ache.
  • Severity: 7 out of 10.
  • Onset and course: came on gradually 2 days ago and has been there all the time since, including at rest and at night.
  • Context: "Nothing unusual happened." No injury, fall, knock, sport or exercise when it started. Only if asked about sitting, travel or being less active: "I've had to work from home the past few months, so I've just been sitting around all day every day."
  • Better or worse: you tried some Panadol, which helped at first but wore off after a few hours. Walking on it makes it slightly worse. It does not come on with walking and go away with rest; it is there all the time.
  • Impact: you are finding it hard to focus on work and to sleep because of the constant pain.

Other symptoms (only if asked):

  • Swelling: you think the left calf looks a bit puffier than the right, and your sock leaves a mark on that side.
  • Warmth: "maybe a little warm". Redness: none.
  • No fever, sweats or shivers. No cuts, scratches, insect bites or bruises on the leg.
  • No sudden tearing or popping feeling in the calf. You can walk on it, with a slight limp.
  • No swelling or lump behind the knee before the pain started. No knee problems.
  • No coldness, paleness, numbness, tingling or weakness in the foot.
  • No shortness of breath, chest pain, cough, coughing up blood, racing heart, dizziness or fainting.
  • No weight loss, night sweats or lumps anywhere.

Past medical history: acne, anxiety (no medicine for it now; you saw a psychologist a few years ago) and you are overweight. No previous blood clots. No surgery, hospital stays, plaster casts or long flights or drives recently.

Women's health (only if asked): you are on the pill and take it every day. Your last period ended about 2 weeks ago and was normal. You do not think you could be pregnant. Never been pregnant.

Medications:

  • Prescription: the oral contraceptive pill (a combined pill with oestrogen, taken for about 8 years for contraception and your skin) and doxycycline for acne, one tablet a day for the last 2 months.
  • Over the counter: Panadol for occasional headaches, and for this pain.
  • No recreational drugs, no supplements.

Allergies: none.

Family history: your mother had her gallbladder removed at 57 and has seasonal asthma. Your father is well and has had some skin cancers removed. Your siblings are well. Nobody in the family has had blood clots, bleeding problems or cancer that you know of.

Social history:

  • Non-smoker, never smoked. Alcohol occasionally, about 2 drinks once a month. No drugs.
  • Accountant, working from home for the past few months.
  • Exercise: you try to walk once a week.
  • Diet: a mix of cooking your own meals and takeaway.
  • You live at home with your parents. Support from your parents and work mates.

Ideas, concerns, expectations:

  • Idea: "I'm not sure what it is. I don't remember injuring that area."
  • Concern: "I'm worried it's something serious and will affect my ability to walk."
  • Expectation: you would like to know what it is and get something to stop the pain so you can sleep and work.

Use plain language and say you do not follow if the candidate uses jargon.

Exam findings (give only when the candidate says what they examine)

  • General: comfortable at rest, walks in with a slight limp. Weight 78 kg, height 165 cm (BMI 28.7). Mild acne on the face.
  • Vital signs: HR 84 regular, BP 118/74 mmHg, RR 16, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.9 °C.
  • Inspection of both legs: the left calf is visibly swollen compared with the right. No redness, streaking, skin breaks, bites or bruising. No visible collateral superficial veins. Both feet pink.
  • Palpation: left calf slightly warmer than the right. Tender along the deep veins of the calf and in the left popliteal fossa. Pitting oedema of the left ankle and lower shin; none on the right.
  • Measurements: calf circumference 10 cm below the tibial tuberosity: left 39.5 cm, right 36.0 cm (3.5 cm difference). Thigh circumference equal on both sides (the whole leg is not swollen).
  • Popliteal fossa and knee: no mass or cyst felt. Knee: full range of movement, no effusion.
  • Calf muscles: no palpable defect; pain on resisted plantarflexion mild; Simmonds-Thompson test normal (Achilles intact). Able to weight bear, with a slight antalgic limp.
  • Arterial and neurological: femoral, popliteal, dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses present and equal on both sides. Capillary refill under 2 seconds. Sensation and power normal.
  • Lymph nodes: no inguinal lymphadenopathy.
  • Chest and heart: chest clear, normal breath sounds. Heart sounds dual, no added sounds. No raised JVP.

check.x: Professionalism
Hand hygiene, clear introduction (name and role as a medical student), confirms Mary's identity and gains consent for the examination.
Uses plain language and an empathic manner, and acknowledges Mary's worry about her walking.
History
Characterises the pain:

kids.x: Site and radiation: left calf only, no radiation.
Onset and course: gradual over 2 days, constant.
Aggravating and relieving factors: worse walking, brief relief from Panadol; pain is not exertional and present at rest.

check.x: Asks about trauma and the context, and elicits the recent immobility (working from home, sitting all day for months).
Asks about features of DVT and PE:

kids.x: Local features: calf swelling, warmth, redness.
PE symptoms: shortness of breath, pleuritic chest pain, cough, haemoptysis, palpitations, dizziness or fainting. Credit if asks about breathlessness and chest pain plus at least one other.

check.x: Screens for VTE risk factors:

kids.x: Oestrogen-containing contraception or HRT, and pregnancy or recent pregnancy (LMP).
Recent surgery, hospitalisation, plaster cast or long-distance travel, and active cancer or constitutional symptoms.

check.x: Explores the associated symptoms of other differentials. Full marks if the candidate screens at least 3 of the 4 differentials below with at least one relevant symptom each:

kids.x: Cellulitis: fever, redness, cuts, bites or broken skin as a portal of entry.
Muscle tear or contusion: sudden tearing sensation during exercise, difficulty weight bearing, bruising.
Dissecting or ruptured Baker's cyst: swelling behind the knee before the calf pain, knee arthritis.
Arterial disease: pain on exertion relieved by rest, pallor, coldness, numbness or weakness.

check.x: Takes the past medical history: acne, anxiety, overweight.
Takes a medication and allergy history: combined oral contraceptive pill, doxycycline, occasional Panadol, no recreational drugs or supplements, no allergies.
Takes a family history, specifically asking about VTE, bleeding disorders and cancer (none).
Takes a social history: smoking, alcohol, occupation, exercise, diet, living situation and support.
Explores ideas, concerns and expectations (no injury she can recall, fear of something serious affecting her walking).
Examination
Requests vital signs including SpO2 and temperature, and examines the chest and heart for signs of PE.
Inspects both legs, comparing sides: swelling, redness, skin breaks, colour and collateral superficial veins.
Palpates both legs:

kids.x: Tenderness along the distribution of the deep veins.
Pitting oedema, comparing the two legs.

check.x: Measures calf circumference on both sides 10 cm below the tibial tuberosity (and compares thigh circumference).
Checks peripheral pulses, capillary refill and sensation in both legs.
Examines the popliteal fossa for a cyst, the knee, and the calf muscles for a palpable defect or pain on resisted plantarflexion (Simmonds-Thompson test to exclude Achilles rupture if relevant).
Interpretation
Interprets the observations as normal (no tachycardia, hypoxia or fever), so no clinical signs of PE or sepsis and she is stable for outpatient care.
Interprets the ultrasound as an acute proximal DVT: a non-compressible left popliteal vein with thrombus extending into the posterior tibial and peroneal veins.
Notes that the femoral veins are patent and that there is no Baker's cyst, muscle tear or superficial thrombophlebitis.
Interprets the bloods: normal haemoglobin, platelets, renal function, liver function and coagulation, so no contraindication to a DOAC; negative beta-hCG, so she is not pregnant.

Identifies the DVT as provoked, mainly by the combined oestrogen-containing pill (a transient hormonal risk factor that will be stopped), with prolonged sitting and being overweight as contributing minor risk factors.

Names the Wells score, scores Mary 3 with the components (deep vein tenderness, calf more than 3 cm larger, pitting oedema), and states that DVT likely or high probability goes straight to compression ultrasound without a D-dimer (D-dimer first only if unlikely).
check.d: Accept the two-level or three-level version. The minus-2 alternative-diagnosis rule is credited but not required.

check.x: Management
Explains the diagnosis to Mary in plain words (a clot in a deep vein of the leg), and addresses her concern about walking if she raises it.

Starts anticoagulation today with a correct regimen (either DOAC is accepted): rivaroxaban 15 mg twice daily with food for 21 days then 20 mg once daily with food, or apixaban 10 mg twice daily for 7 days then 5 mg twice daily; or enoxaparin 1 mg/kg subcut twice daily (or 1.5 mg/kg once daily) with warfarin started and overlapped until INR 2 to 3 on two consecutive days, at least 5 days of enoxaparin. A DOAC is preferred for outpatient care.
Plans 3 months of anticoagulation for a DVT provoked by a transient risk factor, with review before stopping; advises paracetamol not NSAIDs for pain, and to keep walking.
Stops the combined pill and arranges a non-oestrogen method of contraception now, because oestrogen raises clot risk and DOACs must not be taken in pregnancy.
Safety netting

Tells her to call 000 for sudden shortness of breath, chest pain worse on breathing in, coughing up blood, a racing heart or fainting. Credit if names at least 3, including breathlessness and chest pain.
Explains bleeding red flags on a blood thinner and to go to ED: at least 3 of black or bloody stools, blood in urine or vomit, very heavy periods, severe headache or any head injury.
Advises her to go to ED urgently if the leg becomes much more swollen, painful, pale, blue or cold, or the foot goes numb.
Arranges GP review within a week and at 3 months.

part2.lead: Mary had an ultrasound and blood tests at the imaging and pathology centre next door, about 3 hours after you saw her, and has come back to see you early this afternoon. Here are her observations, the ultrasound report and her blood results. On examination this morning: left calf 3.5 cm larger than the right (39.5 vs 36.0 cm, 10 cm below the tibial tuberosity), pitting oedema of the left ankle and shin, tenderness along the deep veins and popliteal fossa, thigh circumference equal, no collateral superficial veins.
part2.patient:
Ask this when the candidate explains the plan, if not already covered:

  • "Do I really have to stop the pill? I need it for my skin and I don't want to get pregnant."

Settle if the candidate answers honestly and clearly.

handover.label: Observations
handover.result: Taken by the practice nurse at the morning visit and again on her return from imaging; room air.
handover.model:
Both sets are normal: HR 84 then 82, BP 118/74 then 120/76 mmHg, RR 16, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.9 then 36.8 °C. All values would sit in the normal (white) area of an adult chart, so no clinical review or rapid response criteria apply.

For Mary: no tachycardia, tachypnoea or hypoxia, so no clinical evidence of PE, and no fever, which makes cellulitis less likely. She is stable and suitable for outpatient management. Normal observations do not exclude a small PE, so she still needs PE safety-netting.

handover.label: Compression ultrasound with Doppler, left leg
handover.result:
Examination: venous duplex ultrasound of the left lower limb (compression ultrasound with colour and spectral Doppler), whole leg. Limited assessment of the right common femoral vein for comparison.

Clinical details: 26-year-old woman, left calf pain and swelling for 2 days. Combined oral contraceptive pill. Prolonged sitting. ?DVT.

Comparison: no previous imaging.

Findings:

  • Left common femoral and femoral veins: fully compressible, normal phasic flow and normal augmentation. No thrombus.
  • Left popliteal vein: distended and non-compressible, filled with hypoechoic intraluminal thrombus. No colour flow (occlusive).
  • Left calf veins: the posterior tibial and peroneal veins are distended and non-compressible, with thrombus continuous with the popliteal thrombus.
  • Left great and small saphenous veins: compressible, no superficial vein thrombosis.
  • Popliteal fossa: no Baker's cyst or fluid collection.
  • Calf soft tissues: subcutaneous oedema. No intramuscular haematoma or muscle tear.
  • Right common femoral vein: compressible with normal phasic flow.

Conclusion: acute occlusive deep vein thrombosis of the left popliteal vein extending into the posterior tibial and peroneal veins (proximal DVT). Femoral veins patent. No Baker's cyst or muscle injury.
handover.model:
Read: the key finding is a non-compressible popliteal vein with thrombus and no flow. Thrombus extends into the posterior tibial and peroneal veins. A distended vein with hypoechoic thrombus suggests an acute clot. The femoral veins are compressible with normal flow, so the clot stops at the popliteal vein. There is no Baker's cyst, muscle tear or superficial thrombosis.

For Mary: acute proximal DVT (popliteal involvement counts as proximal). This confirms the high clinical probability and excludes the other diagnoses this scan can show.

What it changes: she needs full-dose anticoagulation today. Proximal DVT carries a higher risk of PE than isolated distal DVT, so 'watch and rescan' is not an option.

handover.label: Blood results (today)
handover.model:
Read: normal haemoglobin, white cells and platelets, normal electrolytes, creatinine 64 with eGFR over 90, normal ALT and bilirubin, and normal INR and APTT. Serum beta-hCG under 5 IU/L is negative.

For Mary: normal platelets, clotting and liver tests show no laboratory bleeding tendency and no contraindication to anticoagulation. Her creatinine clearance (Cockcroft-Gault, about 145 mL/min) is well above the DOAC thresholds, so no dose change is needed. She is not pregnant, so a DOAC can be used.

What it changes: start rivaroxaban or apixaban today. These are her baseline results. Thrombophilia testing is not indicated after a provoked DVT.

ask: You are now calling your GP supervisor. Please give an ISBAR handover of Mary, including your interpretation of these results.
What is your most likely diagnosis, and what else would you consider? Justify your answer, including the clinical decision rule you would have applied to Mary and how her score decided the next test.
Outline your management of Mary now, here in general practice.
What safety netting and follow-up would you give Mary?

ddx.dx: Acute proximal deep vein thrombosis of the left leg, provoked
ddx.for: Gradual, constant left calf pain with 3.5 cm calf swelling, pitting oedema and deep vein tenderness while on the combined pill after months of sitting, and a non-compressible popliteal vein on ultrasound.
A proximal DVT is the usual source of PE.
ddx.against: No breathlessness, chest pain, cough or haemoptysis, and HR 84 with SpO2 99% on room air.

ddx.for: The calf is swollen, tender and slightly warm.
ddx.against: No fever, redness, streaking or skin break, and a normal white cell count.

ddx.dx: Gastrocnemius or soleus tear or contusion
ddx.for: Calf pain that is worse when walking.
ddx.against: No injury or sudden tearing pain, she weight bears, there is no palpable defect, and the ultrasound shows no tear or haematoma.

ddx.for: Calf pain and swelling with tenderness in the popliteal fossa.
ddx.against: No swelling behind the knee beforehand, a normal knee, and no cyst on ultrasound.

ddx.for: Leg pain that is worse with walking.
ddx.against: Pain is constant at rest, the leg is swollen and warm rather than pale and cold, all pulses are present, and she is a 26-year-old non-smoker.

guide:
In Part 1 the examiner gives findings from the Exam findings only when the candidate says what they examine. Mary gives the immobility history only if asked about sitting, travel or activity. In Part 2, read the lead (which restates the leg examination findings), hand over all three results together and ask the four questions in order. Mary's question about stopping the pill can be put while the candidate answers the management question.

Score the differentials item (History, item 9): full marks if the candidate screens at least 3 of the 4 differentials listed in the item with at least one relevant symptom each. If a candidate performs Homans' sign, do not give credit for it; it is unreliable.

A high-performing candidate elicits the combined pill and the months of sitting, screens for PE symptoms, and measures calf circumference. They recognise an acute proximal DVT on the ultrasound and check the bloods for suitability for a DOAC and for pregnancy. They prescribe a correct DOAC regimen for 3 months, stop the combined pill with a plan for contraception, give specific PE and bleeding red flags, and calculate the Wells score correctly with the pathway.

A borderline candidate misses the pill or the immobility, does not ask about PE symptoms, or orders a D-dimer despite a high Wells score. They may give a vague anticoagulant plan without doses or duration, leave her on the combined pill, or end with "come back if it gets worse".
explain:
Diagnosis and reasoning

Mary has an acute proximal DVT of the left leg. It is provoked, mainly by the combined oestrogen-containing pill (a transient hormonal risk factor that will be stopped), with prolonged sitting while working from home and being overweight as contributing minor risk factors. DVT may cause no symptoms, or unilateral (sometimes bilateral) leg pain, swelling, warmth and redness. The history should cover symptoms of PE and the common risk factors:

  • immobilisation or prolonged hospitalisation, recent surgery or trauma
  • obesity, previous VTE, family history of VTE
  • malignancy or constitutional symptoms suggesting it
  • oral contraceptives or HRT, pregnancy or the postpartum period
  • stroke with hemiplegia or immobility, age over 65, heart failure, inflammatory bowel disease

Differentials

  • Cellulitis: pain, swelling, redness and warmth, often with fever and a portal of entry such as a cut or bite.
  • Gastrocnemius or soleus tear or contusion: a sudden tearing sensation during exercise and difficulty weight bearing.
  • Dissecting or ruptured Baker's cyst: swelling behind the knee before the calf pain.
  • Peripheral vascular disease: pain on exertion. Acute ischaemia gives the 6 Ps: pain, pallor, paraesthesia, perishingly cold, pulselessness and paralysis.
  • Pulmonary embolism: the complication that must be actively excluded by history and observations.

Pre-test probability: the Wells score

Score 1 point each for:

  • paralysis, paresis or a recent plaster cast of a lower limb
  • recently bedridden for more than 3 days, or major surgery within 4 weeks
  • localised tenderness along the deep venous system
  • entire leg swollen
  • calf swelling more than 3 cm compared with the other leg, measured 10 cm below the tibial tuberosity
  • pitting oedema greater in the symptomatic leg
  • collateral non-varicose superficial veins
  • active cancer, or cancer treated within 6 months

Subtract 2 points if an alternative diagnosis is at least as likely as DVT. The original three-level score (Wells 1997) bands 0 or less low, 1 to 2 moderate, 3 or more high. In current practice, including eTG, the two-level version (Wells 2003, which adds a point for previous DVT) is used: DVT unlikely (1 or less) goes to a D-dimer, and a negative D-dimer excludes DVT; DVT likely (2 or more) goes straight to ultrasound. Mary scores 3: tenderness, calf difference of 3.5 cm, pitting oedema. Her sitting at home is a risk factor but does not meet the "bedridden" criterion. She goes straight to ultrasound.

Interpreting the results

Compression ultrasonography with Doppler is the investigation of choice. The diagnostic finding is non-compressibility of an imaged vein. Mary's popliteal vein is distended and non-compressible with occlusive hypoechoic thrombus extending into the calf veins, and the femoral veins are patent. Popliteal involvement makes this a proximal DVT. The scan also excludes a Baker's cyst and a muscle tear. Her observations show no clinical PE. Her baseline bloods are normal and her beta-hCG is negative, so a DOAC is suitable and no dose adjustment is needed.

Management (Therapeutic Guidelines)

Treatment depends on the site of the thrombosis and bleeding risk, but generally means anticoagulation. Options include:

  • subcutaneous low molecular weight heparin, subcutaneous fondaparinux, or unfractionated heparin
  • an oral factor Xa inhibitor: rivaroxaban 15 mg twice daily with food for 21 days, then 20 mg once daily with food; or apixaban 10 mg twice daily for 7 days, then 5 mg twice daily

Warfarin is not appropriate on its own for initial anticoagulation. Stable patients with no features of PE and a low bleeding risk can be treated as outpatients. If ultrasound cannot be done promptly (e.g. within about 4 hours) in a high-probability patient with low bleeding risk, start interim anticoagulation while awaiting the scan. For a VTE provoked by a transient risk factor, 3 months of anticoagulation is usually enough, reviewed before stopping. Thrombophilia testing is not routinely indicated after a provoked event.

Contraception and acne

Oestrogen-containing contraception should be stopped after VTE. Switch straight from the COC to an implant, LNG-IUD or progestogen-only pill (follow FSRH switching and additional-precaution rules), because DOACs must not be taken in pregnancy. Continue doxycycline as planned and review her acne at GP follow-up, adding topical therapy (e.g. adapalene/benzoyl peroxide) because stopping the combined pill may worsen it. Consider apixaban, which carries less heavy menstrual bleeding than rivaroxaban; an LNG-IUD also reduces bleeding. Encourage walking, regular breaks from sitting and gradual weight loss. Use paracetamol rather than NSAIDs for pain.

Safety netting

  • Call 000 for sudden breathlessness, chest pain on breathing, coughing up blood, a racing heart or fainting.
  • Go to ED for signs of bleeding (black or bloody stools, blood in the urine or vomit, very heavy periods), a severe headache or any head injury, or a leg that becomes much more swollen, pale or cold.
  • Follow-up: GP review within a week, then at 3 months to plan stopping anticoagulation. She should tell pharmacists, dentists and other doctors that she is taking an anticoagulant.
points: In unilateral calf pain, ask specifically about immobility, oestrogen-containing contraception, pregnancy, previous or family VTE, cancer and PE symptoms.

Wells score for DVT: in the two-level version used in current practice, DVT unlikely (1 or less) goes to a D-dimer, and a negative D-dimer excludes DVT; DVT likely (2 or more) goes straight to compression ultrasound.
Compression ultrasound with Doppler diagnoses DVT by non-compressibility of an imaged vein; popliteal involvement makes it proximal.

A DOAC (rivaroxaban 15 mg twice daily for 21 days then 20 mg daily, or apixaban 10 mg twice daily for 7 days then 5 mg twice daily) for 3 months treats a provoked DVT. Warfarin alone is not used for initial treatment.
Stop oestrogen-containing contraception after VTE and switch straight to a non-oestrogen method, because DOACs must not be taken in pregnancy.
Safety-net for both PE (call 000) and bleeding on anticoagulation (go to ED).

imaging.caption: Compression ultrasound of Mary's left popliteal vein
